definition:
Christian hope is the confident expectation of what God has promised and has not yet done. It is not a wish that things will turn out well, and it is not optimism about human progress. Its object is God himself and its content is specific: the return of Christ, the resurrection of the dead in their bodies, the judgment of the world in righteousness, and the life of the world to come in a renewed creation. The church's oldest creeds end on exactly this note. The Apostles' Creed confesses 'the resurrection of the body' (in the Latin, carnis resurrectionem, literally 'the resurrection of the flesh'), and the creed of Constantinople in 381 says the church looks for 'the resurrection of the dead, and the life of the world to come'. The branch of theology that studies these things is called eschatology, from the Greek eschatos, 'last'. Because the risen Jesus is the first fruits of this harvest, the hope is not a guess about the future but an extension of something that has already happened in the middle of history. This study traces that hope, and above all the resurrection of the dead, through Scripture; the return of Christ, the new creation, the state of the dead before the resurrection, and final judgment each have their own study.

The Hebrew Bible's main words for hope are verbs of waiting. Qavah means to wait for or look eagerly toward (Psalm 130:5; Isaiah 40:31), and its noun tiqvah, which appears about thirty-four times, means expectation or hope (Job 14:7; Jeremiah 29:11). The same spelling tiqvah is used for the scarlet cord Rahab hung from her window (Joshua 2:18), which has led some preachers to say that hope is 'a cord', but that is a coincidence of spelling and a classic etymological fallacy; in the Joshua passage the word simply means a cord. Yachal, to wait with expectation, and batach, to trust, fill out the picture: hope in the Old Testament is patient, directed waiting on a faithful God. In the New Testament the noun elpis (about fifty times) and the verb elpizō carry the same sense of confident expectation, never mere uncertainty. The key word for the content of the hope is anastasis, 'resurrection', literally a standing up again, used about forty times, alongside the verb egeirō, 'to raise' or 'to wake', which is used both for waking from sleep and for rising from the dead.
ot:
The Old Testament begins with death as an intruder. The man formed from the dust and given the breath of life (Genesis 2:7) is told after his rebellion, “For dust you are, and to dust you shall return” (Genesis 3:19), and the long genealogy of Genesis 5 tolls the refrain 'and he died' over each generation. For most of the Old Testament the dead go down to Sheol, the realm of the dead (the study of death and the intermediate state traces that word), and many psalms speak of death as the end of praise: “It is not the dead who praise the LORD, nor any who descend into silence” (Psalm 115:17). The Old Testament does not rush to comfort. Yet from early on it holds a conviction that will eventually break the silence open. The God of Israel is Lord of death as well as life: “I bring death and I give life; I wound and I heal” (Deuteronomy 32:39), and Hannah sings that “The LORD brings death and gives life; He brings down to Sheol and raises up” (1 Samuel 2:6). Enoch “was no more, because God had taken him away” (Genesis 5:24), Elijah is taken up in a whirlwind (2 Kings 2:11), and Elijah and Elisha each restore a dead child to life (1 Kings 17:17-24; 2 Kings 4:18-37). These are returns to ordinary mortal life rather than resurrection in the later sense, but they show that death does not have the last word where God chooses to speak.

The wisdom books and psalms press the question hardest. Job observes that a felled tree can sprout again at the scent of water, “But a man dies and is laid low; he breathes his last, and where is he?” (Job 14:10), and then asks outright, “When a man dies, will he live again?” (Job 14:14). Five chapters later he declares, “I know that my Redeemer lives, and in the end He will stand upon the earth” (Job 19:25), and that “in my flesh I will see God” (Job 19:26). The Hebrew of verse 26 is notoriously difficult: the phrase rendered 'in my flesh' can also be read 'apart from my flesh', so some interpreters hear a hope of seeing God after bodily death and others a vindication before death, while Christian readers from the early church onward heard in it the resurrection. Several psalms reach beyond the grave. “You will not abandon my soul to Sheol, nor will You let Your Holy One see decay” (Psalm 16:10), a verse Peter and Paul will both apply to Jesus. “God will redeem my life from Sheol, for He will surely take me to Himself” (Psalm 49:15), and “You guide me with Your counsel, and later receive me in glory” (Psalm 73:24). Interpreters differ over how much these verses meant to their first singers, but they show a trust in God that cannot imagine the relationship simply ending.

The prophets turn this trust into promise. Hosea's people say “on the third day He will raise us up, that we may live in His presence” (Hosea 6:2), a picture of national revival, and God later asks, “Where, O Death, are your plagues? Where, O Sheol, is your sting?” (Hosea 13:14). In Ezekiel's valley of dry bones, written to exiles in Babylon after 586 BC who said “our hope has perished” (Ezekiel 37:11), God promises, “I will open your graves and bring you up from them” (Ezekiel 37:12). The vision is first about Israel's restoration from exile, but it chooses the image of bodies re-formed and filled with breath, and it binds the hope to the gift of God's Spirit (Ezekiel 37:14). Isaiah goes further. On the mountain where God spreads a feast for all peoples, “He will swallow up death forever. The Lord GOD will wipe away the tears from every face” (Isaiah 25:8), and a few chapters later, “Your dead will live; their bodies will rise” (Isaiah 26:19).

The clearest statement comes in Daniel: “many who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake, some to everlasting life, but others to shame and everlasting contempt” (Daniel 12:2), and Daniel himself is told, “You will rest, and will arise to your inheritance at the end of the days” (Daniel 12:13). Here resurrection is personal, bodily ('the dust of the earth'), and tied to judgment. Scholars date the book differently: many critical scholars place its final form in the 160s BC, during the persecution under the Seleucid king Antiochus IV, while traditional interpreters hold that it comes from Daniel in the sixth century BC. Scholars also differ on how early Israel's resurrection hope took shape. Many have argued that it arose late, under the pressure of martyrdom; Jon D. Levenson (Resurrection and the Restoration of Israel, 2006) argued that it grows from roots deep in Israel's older faith in a God who gives life and restores his people. By the time of Jesus, the hope was widespread among Jews. The martyr stories of 2 Maccabees 7 (a book in the Catholic and Orthodox Old Testament) have a mother and her sons die confessing that God will raise them. The Pharisees taught the resurrection, while the Sadducees denied it (Acts 23:8; Josephus, Jewish War 2.163-166). The Mishnah later counted denial of the resurrection among the beliefs that forfeit a share in the world to come (m. Sanhedrin 10:1), and the second blessing of the Amidah, the central Jewish daily prayer, praises God as the one who gives life to the dead.
nt:
Jesus took his stand with the resurrection hope of the Pharisees and deepened it. When the Sadducees tried to make it absurd with a riddle about a woman married to seven brothers, he answered, “Aren't you mistaken, because you do not know the Scriptures or the power of God?” (Mark 12:24). The resurrection life is not a continuation of this age's arrangements, since “When the dead rise, they will neither marry nor be given in marriage” (Mark 12:25), and the ground of the hope is God's covenant faithfulness: the God who called himself the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob “is not the God of the dead, but of the living” (Mark 12:27). Luke calls the raised “sons of the resurrection” (Luke 20:36). In John's Gospel Jesus claims to be the one through whom the resurrection comes: “the hour is coming when all who are in their graves will hear His voice and come out” (John 5:28-29), to life or to judgment, and of those the Father gives him he says, “I will raise him up at the last day” (John 6:40). At the tomb of Lazarus, Martha voices the standard Jewish hope, “I know that he will rise again in the resurrection at the last day” (John 11:24), and Jesus relocates it in himself: “I am the resurrection and the life” (John 11:25). His raising of Lazarus, like his other raisings, restores mortal life; it is a sign of the resurrection, not the thing itself.

The thing itself happens first to Jesus. Jewish hope had expected all the righteous to rise together at the end of the age; instead one man rose in the middle of history, in a body that could be touched and that ate (Luke 24:39-43), yet was no longer subject to death. The apostles concluded that the end had begun. Paul calls the risen Christ “the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (1 Corinthians 15:20), using the word aparchē for the first sheaf of the harvest offered to God, which is the pledge that the rest of the harvest will follow. Christ's resurrection is therefore the pattern and the guarantee of his people's; the study of the resurrection of Jesus treats the event itself. The apostles' preaching was about “Jesus and the resurrection” together (Acts 17:18), and when Paul spoke of it in Athens some mocked (Acts 17:32). Before Felix he summed up his hope as “a resurrection of both the righteous and the wicked” (Acts 24:15).

The longest treatment is 1 Corinthians 15. Some in Corinth said “there is no resurrection of the dead” (1 Corinthians 15:12), probably not denying life after death but finding a bodily future unnecessary or distasteful, as many Greeks did. Paul replies that if the dead are not raised then Christ is not raised, faith is futile, and “If our hope in Christ is for this life alone, we are to be pitied more than all men” (1 Corinthians 15:19). Then he answers the question “How are the dead raised? With what kind of body will they come?” (1 Corinthians 15:35) with the image of a seed: what is sown is not the plant that will be, yet the plant grows from the seed, and “God gives it a body as He has designed” (1 Corinthians 15:38). The body is sown perishable and raised imperishable, sown in weakness and raised in power; “It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body” (1 Corinthians 15:44). The phrase 'spiritual body' (sōma pneumatikon) does not mean a body made of spirit, as if it were immaterial. The contrasting word psychikon describes the body animated by ordinary natural life, so the spiritual body is a body wholly animated and governed by the Holy Spirit. The living will not be left behind: “We will not all sleep, but we will all be changed” (1 Corinthians 15:51), and when the mortal puts on immortality, the words of Isaiah 25:8 and Hosea 13:14 are fulfilled. Paul ends not with speculation but with a command to keep working, because “your labor in the Lord is not in vain” (1 Corinthians 15:58).

The rest of the New Testament makes the resurrection the shape of Christian waiting. The Spirit who raised Jesus “will also give life to your mortal bodies” (Romans 8:11), and believers groan “as we wait eagerly for our adoption as sons, the redemption of our bodies. For in this hope we were saved” (Romans 8:23-24). Christ “will transform our lowly bodies to be like His glorious body” (Philippians 3:21). Paul writes to grieving Thessalonians not to forbid their grief but so that they “will not grieve like the rest, who are without hope” (1 Thessalonians 4:13). Hope becomes one of the abiding marks of the Christian life, with faith and love (1 Corinthians 13:13), and it is tested rather than weakened by suffering, since “hope does not disappoint us” (Romans 5:5). Hebrews calls it “an anchor for the soul, firm and secure” (Hebrews 6:19). Peter says God has given believers “new birth into a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead” (1 Peter 1:3) and tells them to be ready to explain “the reason for the hope that is in you” (1 Peter 3:15). John admits how much is unknown, “what we will be has not yet been revealed” (1 John 3:2), while knowing the one thing that matters: “we will be like Him, for we will see Him as He is”. Revelation closes the story with the sea, Death, and Hades giving up their dead (Revelation 20:13) and a world in which “there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain” (Revelation 21:4). How that final resurrection relates to the 'first resurrection' of Revelation 20:4-6 is one of the questions on which the millennial views divide; the site's survey is at /theology/doctrine/last-things.

keyTexts.why: Job, having asked whether a man who dies will live again, declares that his Redeemer lives and that he will see God. The Hebrew of verse 26 is disputed, but the passage became one of the church's great resurrection texts.
The psalmist trusts that God will not abandon him to Sheol or let his Holy One see decay. Peter and Paul both preach it as fulfilled in the resurrection of Jesus (Acts 2:25-31; 13:35-37).
At a feast for all peoples, God swallows up death forever and wipes away tears from every face. Paul quotes it as the last word of 1 Corinthians 15, and Revelation 21 echoes it.
The dead will live and their bodies will rise, and those who dwell in the dust are called to awake and sing. It is among the first Old Testament texts to speak of bodily resurrection in plain words.

The valley of dry bones pictures the exiled nation raised from its graves by God's word and Spirit. It is first a promise of national restoration, told in the language of resurrection, which later readers carried further.
The clearest Old Testament statement of the resurrection of individuals: many who sleep in the dust will awake, some to everlasting life and some to everlasting contempt.
Jesus defends the resurrection against the Sadducees by appealing to the power of God and to his covenant name, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, who is the God of the living.
Jesus claims that the dead will hear his voice and come out of their graves, some to life and some to judgment. The Son holds the authority over both resurrection and judgment.
Martha confesses the Jewish hope of resurrection at the last day, and Jesus answers that he himself is the resurrection and the life. The future hope has a present person at its center.
Paul tells the governor Felix that his hope, shared with his Jewish accusers, is a resurrection of the righteous and the wicked. The resurrection was a Jewish hope before it was a Christian one.
Believers and all creation groan as they wait for the redemption of the body. Paul defines hope as confident waiting for what is not yet seen.

Paul's answer to how the dead are raised: continuity like seed and plant, the contrast of natural and spiritual bodies, the change of the living, and the defeat of death. It ends with a call to steady work.
Christians await a Savior from heaven who will transform their lowly bodies to be like his glorious body. The destiny of the body is transformation, not discarding.
Paul writes to grieving believers that God will bring with Jesus those who have fallen asleep. Hope does not cancel grief; it changes its character.
God has given new birth into a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus and an inheritance that cannot perish. The resurrection of Christ is the ground of the Christian's future.

history:
The early church had to defend the resurrection of the body on two fronts at once: against pagan critics who found it absurd and against Christian teachers who spiritualized it. The letter known as 1 Clement (usually dated about AD 96) illustrates the hope with the turning of night to day, the growth of a seed, and the legend of the phoenix. Justin Martyr and the treatise On the Resurrection transmitted under the name of Athenagoras argued that God who made the body from nothing can remake it. Against the Gnostic teachers, who held that matter was unworthy of God and that salvation meant the soul's escape from the body, Irenaeus of Lyons (Against Heresies, about 180, especially book 5) insisted that the flesh God made, fed by the Eucharist, is capable of receiving eternal life, and Tertullian wrote On the Resurrection of the Flesh (early third century) with the same aim. That is why the baptismal creed of the church at Rome, which grew into the Apostles' Creed, confessed the resurrection of the 'flesh' and not only of the dead. Origen of Alexandria (died about 254) took Paul's 'spiritual body' seriously in a different direction, holding that the risen body keeps the individual's distinctive form while its matter is transformed; Methodius of Olympus wrote against him around 300, and his views became a flashpoint in the Origenist controversies of the late fourth century.

The mature patristic statement came from Augustine. Book 22 of The City of God (completed about 426) defends the resurrection of the flesh against philosophical objection and takes up, with evident care and some reserve, the questions people asked: what age the risen will be (he suggested the age of Christ's maturity), what becomes of those lost at sea or eaten by beasts, and whether the scars of the martyrs will remain as marks of honor. His principle was that God, who made all things from nothing, loses nothing that belongs to the body's identity. Gregory of Nyssa's dialogue On the Soul and the Resurrection, set at the deathbed of his sister Macrina (about 380), gave the Greek church a comparable treatment. The creed of Constantinople (381) closed with the expectation of the resurrection of the dead and the life of the world to come, and the Athanasian Creed, a Latin statement from perhaps the late fifth or sixth century, confesses that all people will rise with their bodies and give account for their deeds. The Fourth Lateran Council (1215) defined that all will rise with their own bodies which they now bear. Thomas Aquinas (died 1274), holding with Aristotle that the soul is the form of the body, taught that a soul without its body is not a complete human person, which gave the resurrection a strong philosophical necessity. Caroline Walker Bynum's The Resurrection of the Body in Western Christianity, 200-1336 (1995) traces how seriously the medieval church took the body's material future.

The Reformation did not dispute the resurrection. The Heidelberg Catechism (1563, Question 57) confesses that the believer's soul is taken to Christ at death and that the believer's own flesh will be raised and reunited with the soul, and the Westminster Confession (1646, chapter 32) teaches that the same bodies will be raised, with different qualities, and united again to their souls. In the modern period the pressure came from another direction. Much Western piety, and much liberal theology, reduced the Christian hope to the immortality of the soul in heaven, and the resurrection of the body faded to a figure of speech. Oscar Cullmann's Ingersoll Lecture at Harvard in 1955, published in 1958 as Immortality of the Soul or Resurrection of the Dead?, argued sharply that the New Testament hope is resurrection and not the Greek idea of an immortal soul; critics thought he overdrew the contrast, but his lecture changed the conversation. Jürgen Moltmann (Theology of Hope, 1964) made the promised future the center of theology, and N. T. Wright's The Resurrection of the Son of God (2003) documented that in the ancient world 'resurrection' meant a new bodily life after a period of death, never merely survival of the soul.

differ.view: One general resurrection at Christ's return
differ.body: Amillennial and postmillennial Christians hold that the righteous and the wicked are raised together at the one return of Christ, followed at once by the last judgment and the new creation. Jesus speaks of a single hour when all who are in their graves come out, some to life and some to judgment (John 5:28-29); Paul speaks of one resurrection of the righteous and the wicked (Acts 24:15); Daniel places both destinies in one awakening (Daniel 12:2). The 'first resurrection' of Revelation 20:4-6 is read as the new birth or as the faithful dead living and reigning with Christ in the intermediate state, so the one bodily resurrection remains at the end. This has been the reading of the Catholic, Lutheran, and Reformed confessional traditions since Augustine.

differ.view: Two resurrections separated by the thousand years
differ.body: Premillennial Christians, both historic and dispensational, hold that the righteous are raised at Christ's return and the rest of the dead only after the thousand years of Revelation 20. They note that the same verb, 'came to life', is used for both groups in Revelation 20:4-5, so both should be bodily resurrections, and that Paul describes an order, “each in his own turn” (1 Corinthians 15:23), in which the resurrection of Christ's people comes at his coming and 'the end' follows. They read the one 'hour' of John 5 as an era, as John uses 'hour' for the present age of new life in the same passage (John 5:25). Irenaeus and Justin held a reign of Christ between the resurrection of the just and the end, and George Eldon Ladd gave the view its modern scholarly form.

Many Christians, following Tertullian, Augustine, the Fourth Lateran Council (1215), and the Westminster Confession, hold that the risen body is materially the same body that was buried, transformed in its qualities. They point to the empty tomb: Jesus' own body did not stay in the grave, and the risen body bore the wounds of the crucifixion (John 20:27). If the body laid in the grave played no part in the resurrection, they argue, the tomb need not have been empty, and the resurrection of 'the flesh' in the creed would lose its meaning. God, who made the world from nothing, is not hindered by the scattering of the body's elements.

differ.view: Continuity of the person without the same matter
differ.body: Other Christians who confess the bodily resurrection hold that personal identity does not depend on reassembling the same particles, since the matter of a living body is exchanged many times over in a lifetime. They lean on Paul's seed image, in which the plant is continuous with the seed but not made of its material (1 Corinthians 15:36-38), and on his contrast of perishable and imperishable bodies. Origen held a version of this, in which the soul keeps the body's distinctive form; in modern times the physicist and theologian John Polkinghorne described the soul as the pattern that God will remember and re-embody (The God of Hope and the End of the World, 2002). Defenders affirm the empty tomb in Jesus' case, and see it as the sign that the old creation is taken up into the new rather than discarded.

errors:
The church has rejected the denial of the resurrection in both its ancient forms: the Sadducees' denial that the dead rise at all (Mark 12:18), and the Christian teachers who said the resurrection was spiritual and “has already occurred” (2 Timothy 2:18), whom Paul says undermine the faith. The Gnostic teachers of the second century, who held that the body is a prison the soul escapes, were answered by Irenaeus and Tertullian and by the creed's confession of the resurrection of the flesh. The same error returns whenever Christian hope is reduced to the soul going to heaven at death and staying there forever. Heaven at death is a real comfort in the New Testament, but it is not the final hope; a gospel that saves only souls quietly concedes that death wins over the body God made and called good.

The church has also refused to let hope become something smaller than itself. It is not optimism, the belief that history will improve under its own power, and it is not a technique for feeling better. It is not a promise that believers will be spared suffering or made prosperous in this life; Paul sets the hope precisely within suffering (Romans 5:3-5; 8:18). Nor is it a license for speculation. The New Testament answers the question of the resurrection body with a seed, a contrast, and a confession of what has not yet been revealed (1 John 3:2), and Augustine's own discussions of the risen body were offered with reserve. When curiosity about the details crowds out the certainty of the main thing, the church has judged that something has gone wrong.
life:
The resurrection gives weight to the body and to time. If the body is to be raised, then what is done in and to bodies matters: how people eat and rest, how they treat the sick, the disabled, and the aged, how they honor the dead. Christians have buried their dead with care from the beginning, and the English word 'cemetery' comes through Latin from the Greek koimētērion, 'a sleeping place', because the first Christians expected those laid there to wake. Hope also reshapes grief. Paul does not tell the bereaved not to grieve; he tells them not to grieve without hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13), and a Christian funeral can hold tears and confidence in the same room without pretending either one away.

Hope changes how a person bears suffering and how they work. The New Testament never uses the resurrection to make present pain unreal; it says present sufferings are not worth comparing with the glory to come (Romans 8:18), which is a different claim. And it says that work done in the Lord is not wasted (1 Corinthians 15:58), so ordinary faithfulness, the kind no one notices, is not lost when the one who did it dies. Prayer, in this light, is hope spoken aloud. It asks for what God has promised and has not yet given, and it waits with patience because the one it waits for has already been raised.
questions: The Old Testament speaks honestly about death as silence before it speaks of resurrection. What do texts like Psalm 88 and Job 14 add to the Christian hope, and why might it matter that the Bible does not skip them?
Paul calls the risen Christ the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep. How does the resurrection of one man in the middle of history change what Christians expect at the end?
If the final hope is the resurrection of the body and not only the soul's life in heaven, what difference should that make to how Christians treat their own bodies, the sick, and the dead?
